Wealth concentration: read the household share, the group mean and the missing detail

Compare dated official wealth-group averages, derive approximate group shares, and trace cumulative wealth only at the boundaries the published extract supports.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 5 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Choose a source year. Compare the measures.

Published average net worth per household · Q4 2025$1,078,642
Approximate derived net-worth share of the top 20%65.70%
Approximate derived net-worth share of the bottom 40%3.03%

Dated public extract from Statistics Canada’s Distributions of Household Economic Accounts release of 13 April 2026, reviewed 25 October 2026. The selector chooses Q4 2024 or Q4 2025; it does not project to a later date. Mean net worth is nominal assets less liabilities per household, not a median or available cash. The release combines the lowest two wealth quintiles into a bottom-40% group; the other three groups each represent 20%. For the share and cumulative charts, multiply each rounded published group mean by its population share, then divide by the sum of those weighted amounts. Normalising that weighted sum makes the four approximate derived shares add to 100%. The Q4 2025 weighted mean is CAD 1,078,641.80, versus the published CAD 1,078,642; the 20-cent difference is rounding. Source estimates involve data, models and assumptions and may be revised. No confidence bounds are supplied by this release table and none are invented. Within-group wealth distributions, individual households’ transitions, cash availability, inflation-adjusted changes and investment returns are not measured here.

The central idea

A group’s average wealth and its share of national wealth answer different questions. Neither reveals a family’s usable cash or the distribution hidden inside that group.

01

Read the reference quarter and the ranking variable first

A statement about the wealthiest 20% describes households ranked by net worth. It does not identify the highest-income 20%, the oldest 20% or the households with the largest bank deposits. The sorting variable belongs beside the percentage before any planning interpretation is attempted.

This guide uses Statistics Canada’s release table 3 published on 13 April 2026. It contains average net worth per household for the fourth quarters of 2024 and 2025. The selector changes between those two dated snapshots; it does not estimate a current account balance or create a later observation.

The source groups the least wealthy 40% together and shows the next three wealth quintiles separately. A quintile represents one-fifth of the household distribution, while that combined first group represents two-fifths. The four rows therefore have different household weights even though they occupy equal space in a chart.

02

A group average is neither its entry threshold nor its median

For Q4 2025, the published mean is CAD 81,650 within the bottom 40%, CAD 526,185 within the third quintile, CAD 1,160,145 within the fourth quintile and CAD 3,543,579 within the top quintile. The published all-household mean is CAD 1,078,642.

The top-group mean does not tell you the minimum net worth required to enter that group. It also does not tell you the net worth of its middle household. A few very large values can affect an average substantially, and these grouped means do not reveal the observations needed to reconstruct a median, a percentile threshold or an individual distribution.

Net worth is a balance-sheet amount: assets less liabilities. It can contain property and other assets whose value cannot be spent immediately without a transaction. A wealth-group mean therefore cannot be copied into a household cash plan as if it were an available bank balance.

03

Use household weights when moving from group means to approximate shares

To derive a group’s contribution to the overall mean, multiply its published mean by its household weight. For the top group in Q4 2025, the contribution is 20% × CAD 3,543,579 = CAD 708,715.80. For the combined bottom group, it is 40% × CAD 81,650 = CAD 32,660.

Adding the four weighted contributions gives CAD 1,078,641.80. That is 20 cents below the separately published all-household mean, reflecting rounding in the displayed inputs. The website divides each contribution by this weighted sum so that the four approximate derived wealth shares add to 100%.

The results are about 65.70% for the top 20% and 3.03% for the bottom 40%. The accompanying release describes those shares at rounded headline precision as 65.7% and 3.0%. The website’s extra decimal place is arithmetic from rounded means, not evidence of a more precise official estimate.

The grouped chart places household shares beside wealth shares. A bar at 20% in the first series and about 65.70% in the second uses two different denominators: households and net worth. It does not mean that 65.70% of households are in the top quintile.

04

Trace only the cumulative boundaries the extract actually provides

The cumulative chart begins at zero, then adds the wealth shares at 40%, 60%, 80% and 100% of households, ordered from least to most wealthy. The equality reference is a diagonal: under equal net worth per household, a given household share would hold the same share of wealth.

The displayed curve is a grouped-boundary picture. Straight connecting segments help locate the known endpoints but do not recover what happens inside each group. In particular, this extract has no separate 20% boundary. Filling it in with half the bottom-40% share would silently assume away within-group inequality.

The release explains that the lowest two quintiles are combined because the lowest quintile’s average liabilities exceeded its assets. A positive average for the combined bottom 40% therefore does not establish that its least wealthy households have positive net worth. The missing detail matters.

This chart does not calculate an individual-level Lorenz curve or a Gini coefficient. Computing such a statistic from the few straight segments and presenting it as the country’s actual inequality measure would give the unobserved within-group distribution an unwarranted role.

05

A rise in a group mean is not an investment return for its members

The final chart retains the source’s rounded changes in group mean net worth from Q4 2024 to Q4 2025: 2.1% for the bottom 40%, 3.2% for the third quintile, 4.4% for the fourth and 6.0% for the top quintile. It compares the same quarter of two years and stays fixed when the snapshot selector changes.

Those figures do not show what happened to every household that started in a particular group. Households can move between groups, and a group’s net worth can change through asset values, saving, borrowing and changes in its composition. The chart is a comparison of group averages at two dates, rather than an account statement following the same investors.

The values are nominal. They have not been adjusted for inflation. They should also not be read as a return that a family could earn by adopting the financial habits or assets associated with a higher-wealth group.

06

Keep estimation limits visible beside the concentration story

The release’s notes describe a distributional economic-account system using different data inputs, models and assumptions, with some components relying on information from earlier periods. These are estimates that can be revised. The release table provides no confidence bounds for the selected means, so none are drawn or inferred here.

The grouping is useful for describing concentration at the supported level of detail. It does not establish why an individual household has a particular amount of wealth, forecast where that household will rank later or show its ability to meet next month’s expenses.

For a personal plan, prepare a separate list of assets, debts, access conditions and dated cash needs. Distinguish property value from net sale proceeds, a restricted asset from cash available now, and a debt balance from the payment calendar. A national wealth share provides context for that work; it does not replace it.

  1. Record the reference date and the variable used to rank households.
  2. Keep a group mean separate from a threshold, median or share.
  3. Use the correct group weights and disclose rounding in derived shares.
  4. Leave unsupported within-group detail unknown.
  5. Build the household’s own liquidity plan from its own evidence.
